Within the broader NYSE Composite, the healthcare giant is attracting renewed attention because its recent share-price recovery has not completely removed the valuation discount visible across several earnings-based measures. As a major  Healthcare Stock, UnitedHealth Group combines insurance operations with a large healthcare-services platform, making its earnings profile closely tied to medical costs, operational efficiency, regulatory conditions, and the performance of Optum. UnitedHealth Group has regained meaningful ground during the year, changing the tone around a company that previously faced considerable pressure. The recovery matters because it shows that market sentiment can improve even while questions surrounding medical costs, regulatory scrutiny, and operational execution remain unresolved. The recent advance has also created a more interesting valuation debate. Rather than simply asking whether the company can recover, the market is now weighing whether the current valuation still leaves room for further improvement if earnings stabilize and the broader business regains consistency. That distinction is important for a mature healthcare company of UnitedHealth Groups scale. A recovery in the share price can reduce the apparent discount without necessarily eliminating it. The company still operates through businesses with substantial scale, recurring healthcare demand, extensive provider relationships, and diversified services. If those characteristics translate into steadier earnings and stronger margins, the valuation case could become more compelling. At the same time, continued cost pressure or weaker execution could keep the market from assigning a richer earnings multiple. An earnings-based valuation framework continues to place UnitedHealth Group in an interesting position. The companys earnings multiple remains slightly below the broader healthcare sector and below the level associated with comparable large healthcare businesses. That relative discount is notable because UnitedHealth Group possesses considerable scale and operates across several parts of the healthcare system rather than relying solely on traditional health insurance activities. The valuation gap becomes more significant when compared with a modelled fair earnings multiple. The framework discussed in the source material places a considerably higher multiple on the company than the level currently reflected by the market. Such a gap does not guarantee that the valuation will move toward the modelled level, but it does highlight a disconnect between the companys current earnings valuation and the value implied by assumptions around profitability, scale, industry position, and operating performance. For the valuation discount to remain meaningful, however, the underlying business needs to demonstrate greater consistency. A lower multiple can reflect attractive value, but it can also reflect uncertainty surrounding earnings quality or future operating conditions. UnitedHealth Group therefore faces an important test: demonstrating that current challenges are manageable rather than structural. Optum is central to the UnitedHealth Group story because it extends the company beyond conventional health insurance and into healthcare services, pharmacy solutions, technology-enabled care, and provider operations. Its broad reach gives the group multiple avenues for generating earnings, while also creating significant operational complexity. The current focus on Optum is connected to margin repair and efficiency. When healthcare costs rise or operating conditions become more complicated, margins can come under pressure across different parts of the organization. Improving workflows, strengthening technology infrastructure, and increasing operational efficiency can therefore have an important effect on the overall financial profile. The challenge is that a large integrated healthcare platform cannot be transformed instantly. Changes across provider operations, pharmacy services, technology systems, and clinical workflows require careful execution. If efficiency improvements begin to produce more stable margins, confidence in the wider business could improve. If cost pressures remain elevated, the valuation discount may continue to reflect those concerns. The transaction involving an interest in certain Florida WellMed clinics adds another dimension to the companys restructuring efforts. WellMed is part of the healthcare-services ecosystem associated with Optum, with a focus on coordinated care and provider relationships. The transaction with TPG changes the ownership structure surrounding those clinics and could support greater capital efficiency as UnitedHealth Group works through its broader operational reset. The significance of the transaction extends beyond the immediate restructuring. UnitedHealth Group has been navigating a complicated environment in which medical costs, provider economics, and healthcare utilization patterns can influence profitability. Adjusting the structure of selected operations may help management concentrate resources where they can generate stronger economic returns while reducing pressure from areas requiring substantial operational attention. The longer-term effect will depend on execution. Capital efficiency can strengthen the financial profile, but the broader business still needs to demonstrate that changes across Optum can translate into sustainable margin improvement. Healthcare insurers operate in an environment where medical utilization can change rapidly. Higher utilization, more expensive treatments, changes in care patterns, and increased provider costs can all affect margins. UnitedHealth Group is therefore particularly sensitive to developments in medical spending because of the scale of its insurance operations. The issue is especially important following a period in which cost pressures have received greater market attention. If medical expenses stabilize while premium and service economics remain healthy, earnings visibility could improve. If utilization remains elevated, however, the company may face additional pressure on margins. This creates a balancing act for UnitedHealth Group. The company needs to maintain attractive healthcare coverage while managing the cost of providing that coverage. Its integrated structure can provide advantages because Optum offers services across different parts of the healthcare ecosystem, but that structure also means that weakness in a major operating area can influence the broader financial picture. Technology is becoming increasingly important to UnitedHealth Groups operational strategy. Healthcare organizations generate enormous amounts of information across claims, clinical records, pharmacy services, provider networks, and patient interactions. Improving the way those systems communicate can help reduce administrative friction and support more efficient workflows. UnitedHealth Group has been expanding technology capabilities across its healthcare operations, including tools designed to support physicians and improve digital engagement. Greater automation and better data integration could help reduce administrative burdens while improving the efficiency of care delivery. The financial importance of technology lies in execution rather than the technology itself. Successful implementation could support productivity and margins, while poorly executed changes could add complexity and cost. The market is therefore likely to pay close attention to whether technology initiatives produce measurable operational improvements across the broader organization. Regulation remains one of the most important external factors affecting UnitedHealth Group. Large healthcare companies operate under extensive federal and state oversight, with policy decisions capable of influencing reimbursement, insurance practices, pharmacy services, provider relationships, and healthcare costs. Greater scrutiny can affect how the market values healthcare companies even when underlying operations remain resilient. UnitedHealth Groups scale and integration provide significant competitive advantages, but they also make the company highly visible to policymakers and regulators. The company must therefore balance efficiency with compliance while continuing to serve a broad customer base. Any meaningful regulatory changes could alter the economics of particular business lines. That uncertainty helps explain why valuation comparisons should be considered alongside operational and policy factors rather than viewed in isolation. UnitedHealth Groups scale is one of its defining characteristics. The company operates across insurance and healthcare services, giving it access to a broad ecosystem of members, providers, pharmacies, clinicians, and technology platforms. That scale can create efficiencies that smaller competitors may struggle to replicate. It can also support data-driven healthcare management and broader service integration. The combination of insurance and healthcare services provides opportunities to coordinate care and improve operational efficiency across different parts of the healthcare system. However, scale can also introduce complexity. Large organizations must manage numerous business lines, regulatory requirements, technology systems, and provider relationships. The current valuation debate partly reflects whether UnitedHealth Group can convert its considerable scale into stronger and more consistent profitability. The recent share-price recovery has improved sentiment, but it has also raised the standard for future execution. After a meaningful recovery, the market may become less focused on the possibility of stabilization and more focused on evidence that the improvement can continue. That makes upcoming earnings performance particularly important. Continued margin repair at Optum, controlled medical costs, and stronger operating efficiency could reinforce the recovery narrative. Conversely, renewed cost pressure or weaker performance across healthcare services could challenge the valuation case. The company therefore sits at an interesting point. The earlier weakness has already created room for a recovery, while the subsequent share-price improvement means that future progress will need to be supported by tangible business performance rather than sentiment alone. A stronger valuation case would likely require improvement across several connected areas of the business. Better Optum margins would be important because they could demonstrate that operational changes are translating into improved profitability. Stabilizing medical costs would also help provide greater visibility into insurance earnings. Further efficiency gains from technology and healthcare integration could provide another layer of support. UnitedHealth Group does not need to rely on a single business line to strengthen its financial profile. Instead, improvements across insurance, provider services, pharmacy operations, and technology could collectively create a more durable earnings foundation. The WellMed restructuring also adds another factor. If the revised ownership structure contributes to improved capital efficiency and operational focus, it could reinforce the broader effort to strengthen the business. Several factors could prevent the market from assigning a higher valuation multiple. Regulatory uncertainty remains a major consideration, particularly because healthcare policy can change the economics of large insurers and healthcare-services businesses. Medical-cost inflation and utilization trends are another concern. If healthcare expenses remain elevated, margin improvement could take longer than expected. Optum execution is also important because weakness in that platform could offset strength elsewhere in the group. Concentration and integration risks deserve attention as well. UnitedHealth Group benefits from its broad healthcare ecosystem, but that interconnected structure means operational issues can have wider implications. The market may continue applying a valuation discount until there is clearer evidence that efficiency initiatives and cost controls are producing consistent results. UnitedHealth Groups story is no longer simply about recovery from earlier weakness. The latest phase is increasingly about whether the company can convert operational improvements into a more durable earnings profile while maintaining its competitive position across the healthcare system. The valuation framework remains supportive because the earnings multiple is below broader sector and peer benchmarks, while the modelled fair multiple sits considerably higher. Yet valuation alone cannot determine the direction of a large healthcare company. The market will ultimately focus on earnings quality, margin development, medical-cost trends, regulatory conditions, and the effectiveness of the Optum reset. That creates a more nuanced picture. UnitedHealth Group may still appear inexpensive through certain valuation lenses, but the discount exists alongside genuine operating questions. The key issue is whether those questions gradually become less significant as the business demonstrates stronger execution. UnitedHealth Group remains one of the most important names in the American healthcare landscape because its operations span insurance, healthcare services, pharmacy solutions, technology, and provider networks. That breadth gives the company substantial scale while also making its financial performance sensitive to developments across multiple areas. The recent recovery has brought the valuation discussion back into focus. The company does not need to rely solely on market sentiment to strengthen its position. Improvements in Optum efficiency, better cost management, disciplined capital allocation, and continued technology development could provide the operational foundation required for a stronger financial profile. At the same time, regulatory scrutiny and healthcare-cost pressures remain part of the equation. The next stage of the story will therefore depend less on the recovery itself and more on whether UnitedHealth Group can demonstrate that its underlying operations are becoming more efficient and predictable. Earnings improved, guidance was raised, and medical costs began moving lower. But a September 9 stake sale involving Optum Health shifted attention toward whether the recovery could support the expectations already built into the stock. A stake sale in its troubled Optum Health division sent shares down roughly 3%, exposing the gap between what has recovered and what investors are still waiting to see. UNH’s insurance business has stabilised, but the premium valuation it commands still depends on whether Optum Health can deliver the next stage of growth. For managed care insurers, the medical cost ratio (MCR) measures how much premium revenue goes toward healthcare claims. A lower ratio leaves more room for profit. For UNH, MCR became the clearest measure of whether the post-pandemic cost surge was reversing. The ratio reached 89.4% in Q2 2025, squeezing margins and contributing to a decline of more than 40% from its 2024 peak near $600. The broader managed care sector faced similar pressure as healthcare utilisation increased, but UNH’s scale meant its exposure was larger. By the first half of 2026, the MCR had improved to 85.3%, down from 87.1% a year earlier. That recovery explains much of the stock rebound. It also explains why September’s selloff mattered. Investors are now looking beyond cost recovery and toward whether UNH’s higher-value businesses can justify the premium built into the share price. The improvement in UNH’s core insurance business is genuine. MCR fell 270 basis points in Q2 2026, while full-year adjusted EPS guidance was raised to $19.50–$20.00. At the midpoint, that represents roughly 21% year-over-year earnings growth. The recovery, however, has been concentrated in the insurance business. The next stage of UNH’s valuation depends on Optum. Optum is the reason UNH trades above traditional insurers. The division generated $65.7 billion in Q2 revenue and $4 billion in operating earnings, supported by strength in OptumRx and Optum Insight. These businesses give UNH exposure beyond insurance through pharmacy services, healthcare data, and technology infrastructure. That broader platform is why investors value UnitedHealth differently from traditional managed care companies. The challenge is that Optum’s businesses are not all recovering at the same pace. The pressure is concentrated in Optum Health’s care delivery business. UnitedHealth had already signalled in January 2026 that Optum Health was undergoing a deliberate restructuring — scaling back from underperforming markets and ending provider contracts that were not aligned with its value-based care model. The TPG partnership in September fits that same direction: rather than running every clinic network internally, UNH is bringing in focused partners for specific geographies while retaining equity exposure. $UNH UnitedHealth has sold an interest in some of its Florida WellMed/Optum Health clinics to private-equity firm TPG, as it works to recover from last year’s profit collapse.CFO Wayne DeVeydt said the deal isn’t about raising cash, but bringing in a local partner that can help… pic.twitter.com/sjiU48PYgV CFO Wayne DeVeydt described the arrangement as a local partnership rather than a capital raise, designed to bring operational focus to a segment that needs it — consistent with Optum CEO Dr. Patrick Conway’s earlier framing that the division is concentrating on markets where it has the complementary infrastructure to actually succeed. The move can be interpreted in two ways: disciplined capital allocation to accelerate improvement in a struggling segment, or as evidence that Optum Health requires more support than investors previously expected. Either interpretation leads to the same conclusion: Optum Health is now central to whether UNH can justify its premium. UNH trades at a meaningful premium to the sector average. That premium reflects more than its insurance business. Investors are paying for a company that combines healthcare scale with pharmacy services, data capabilities, and a broader healthcare services platform through Optum. The challenge is that a premium multiple leaves less room for delays. The market is no longer only assessing whether UNH can recover from higher medical costs. It is assessing whether businesses supporting that premium can deliver stronger profitability. Three factors will determine whether the valuation gap remains justified: The valuation gap becomes clearer when compared with other large managed care names. Cigna and CVS are recovering from their own challenges, but their earnings profiles and risks differ from United Healthcare’s. Cigna currently sits in a more insulated position. Its exit from Medicare Advantage reduced exposure to one of the sector’s biggest cost pressures, while Evernorth has become a larger earnings contributor. CVS trades at a lower valuation, but its recovery path remains longer due to Medicare Advantage costs, reimbursement pressure, and legacy litigation. UNH sits between the two. It has stronger infrastructure and more recovery opportunities, but the market is also demanding more proof from businesses that justify its premium. UNH’s valuation makes it sensitive to earnings updates, margin commentary, and policy developments. The September 9 decline showed that investors are reacting not only to current results, but also to confidence in the recovery timeline. A company can continue reporting improving fundamentals while the stock remains vulnerable if expectations move faster than execution. The analyst consensus remains positive, with a 12-month average target of $475, representing around 21% upside from levels near $391. The bear case target sits at $313, implying roughly 20% downside. The wide range reflects uncertainty over how quickly UNH can complete its recovery. UNH has repaired much of the damage caused by rising medical costs. The next catalyst will come from whether Optum Health can translate its strategic position into stronger margins. Until that happens, the stock is likely to remain sensitive to earnings updates, healthcare cost trends, and any sign that the recovery timeline is shifting. title: UNH Announces Manufacturing Company Partnerships - CBIA
content: The University of New Haven has signed master partnership agreements with four manufacturing companies, expanding its push to link academic research with industry needs. The new partners are Medtronic, ARBURG, Sheffield Pharmaceuticals, and Sailion. The deals run through the university’s Elevation Center, which acts as a single entry point for companies seeking access to campus talent and expertise. The agreements span advanced manufacturing, medical technology, pharmaceuticals, and emerging technologies. Each is structured to let companies tap different parts of the university, from engineering labs to business faculty, depending on their needs. Some partnerships are already moving into specific work. Medtronic is exploring a portfolio of projects involving artificial intelligence, data analytics, digital engineering, biomedical testing, manufacturing quality, and predictive analytics. The company is also looking at supply chain resilience work through the university’s National Center for Supply Chain Intelligence. Sheffield Pharmaceuticals is evaluating collaborations in marketing strategy and consumer insights, chemistry and formulation research, and supply-chain optimization, drawing on faculty across the business school and sciences. ARBURG, an injection-molding machinery and automation manufacturer, has launched its first project: a faculty-led sales analytics initiative. Students and faculty will analyze customer and market data to build an ideal customer profile and support data-informed business development strategies. Sailion is joining the partnership network as well, with the university describing early-stage discussions on innovation and workforce collaboration. The university frames the agreements as part of a wider effort to position the Elevation Center as a regional hub connecting employers with schools, workforce boards, and government agencies across Connecticut. “Companies should not have to navigate a fragmented landscape of programs, institutions, and resources,” said Paul Lavoie, vice president of corporate partnerships at UNH. The university expects the partnerships to produce applied research projects, internships, and workforce training programs. “Our role is to understand the challenge, assemble the right partners, and deliver solutions.” The university said it expects the partnerships to produce applied research projects, internships, workforce training programs, and sponsored student engagements over time. title: “Farming the ocean”: UNH-led aquaculture project aims to boost domestic seafood production - Boston 25 News
content: “Farming the ocean”: UNH-led aquaculture project aims to boost domestic seafood production PORTSMOUTH, N.H.  — Just off the coast of Portsmouth, a floating fish farm measuring 50 feet by 30 feet is helping researchers test what they believe could be the future of seafood production in the United States. The offshore aquaculture facility, operated by the University of New Hampshire’s Center for Sustainable Seafood Systems, produces roughly 20,000 pounds of steelhead trout while serving as a model for expanding domestic seafood farming across the country. “Aquaculture is farming the ocean,” said Michael Chambers, a research professor at UNH. The fish raised at the facility are steelhead trout, a species that looks and tastes similar to salmon. The fish begin their lives in inland facilities in New Hampshire’s Lakes Region before being transferred offshore when they weigh just a few ounces. Researchers allow the fish to grow to about 5 to 6 pounds before harvesting them for local markets, including seafood retailers in Portsmouth and the Boston area. A small crew regularly visits the floating farm to feed the fish by hand rather than relying on automated systems. “One of the benefits of that, as opposed to using auto-feeders, is that we have eyes on the fish,” said research project manager Mike Doherty. “We’re able to visually see how quickly the fish are eating.” The fish are fed a specially formulated diet designed to provide the proper balance of protein and fats. While aquaculture can provide a steady supply of seafood, critics have long raised concerns about the environmental impact of concentrating large numbers of fish in a small area. Researchers at the Portsmouth site say they are taking steps to address those concerns. Surrounding the floating pens are mussel droppers which are made up of the mollusks, kelp and seaweed. “The mussels uptake organic nutrients and the seaweeds uptake inorganic nutrients, so it’s all maintaining a healthy balance of nutrient management in the water,” said operations manager Eric Berghahn. Researchers also conduct regular water-quality testing and maintain monitoring equipment downstream from the facility to track environmental conditions. “We’re a very small scale here,” Berghahn said. “In this way it could be extrapolated out to a larger-scale concept for a larger operation.” The project’s success has attracted national attention. UNH was recently selected by the federal government to help oversee a broader effort to expand aquaculture in U.S. waters. Researchers have already helped establish a similar operation near an island off the coast of Alabama, with additional projects planned in Hawaii and California. Chambers said the goal is to increase the nation’s ability to produce its own seafood rather than relying heavily on imports. “Deploying aquaculture systems to be more competitive on a global basis, but to start to really produce domestic seafood, which has not really happened here in the ocean in the United States,” Chambers said. Local seafood businesses say consumers have embraced the product. “They love it,” said Rich Pettigrew, owner of Seaport Fish Company in Rye, New Hampshire. “It’s an alternative to other salmon and steelhead products, but it’s got the story behind it of being a local product.” Pettigrew believes aquaculture will play an increasingly important role as wild fish populations face growing pressure and seafood demand continues to rise. “The future of seafood is going to be aquaculture,” he said. “With the declining numbers of wild seafood and the supply and demand that we have here in the U.S., aquaculture is the future to sustain the amount of people that will eat seafood.” Researchers say another benefit of offshore fish farming is flexibility. As ocean temperatures continue to warm, facilities like the outside Portsmouth harbor can be relocated farther offshore or farther north, allowing operators to maintain conditions that are better suited for fish growth. title: Did Berkshire Sell UNH Stock Too Early? Retail Traders Think So – Call Its Exit ‘Way Overblown’ - Stocktwits
content: Shares of UnitedHealth Group (UNH) slid 4% in overnight trading on Monday after Berkshire Hathaway confirmed that it fully exited its position in the health insurer during the first quarter, sparking aggressive dip-buying chatter among retail traders. UNH stock logged its seventh straight week of gains after rising about 4% last week. Berkshire disclosed in its latest regulatory filings on Friday that it sold its entire 5.04 million-share stake in UNH during the quarter ended March 31, marking one of the most closely watched portfolio changes under new Berkshire CEO Greg Abel. Berkshire also exited positions in companies including Visa, Mastercard, Amazon and Domino's Pizza, while simultaneously building a new roughly $2.65 billion stake in Delta Air Lines. The UnitedHealth investment was originally made in the second quarter of 2025, when Berkshire accumulated shares during one of the stock’s sharpest selloffs in years. Berkshire’s position was later valued at $1.6 billion. UnitedHealth traded mostly between $250 and $290 during the first quarter as investors remained concerned about Medicare Advantage reimbursement pressure, rising medical costs, and uncertainty about Optum Health's margins. By March 31, UNH closed at $270.59 before staging one of the strongest recoveries in the Dow Jones Industrial Average over the following weeks. The stock surged toward the $400 level after stronger-than-expected first quarter earnings, improved Medicare reimbursement, and bullish guidance helped revive investor sentiment around the healthcare giant. UNH has climbed 45% since Feb. 10, making it one of the best-performing Dow components during the rebound period. The rally accelerated further after UnitedHealth said Optum Health was “performing better than expected, sooner than expected.” Retail traders on Stocktwits largely brushed off Berkshire’s exit, with many arguing the conglomerate sold before UnitedHealth’s strongest rebound phase. Sentiment on the platform improved to ‘neutral’ from ‘bearish’ levels a week ago amid over a 200% jump in chatter over the past week. One trader highlighted Berkshire’s timing around the first-quarter lows. “$UNH traded in the $250-$290 range during Q1, where Berkshire fully exited its position,” the user said. “That means they sold between $250-$290 and completely missed the ~+55% move in just 6 weeks.” A separate trader said, “not gonna buy since I was adding in 250-270s, but way overblown reaction. New leadership at brk is just realigning w new goals post buffet” Several retail investors also mocked Berkshire’s leadership transition under Abel and said that the firm exited too early. “So let me understand- Medicare reimbursement rates ended up being higher, great Q1 earnings, rotation towards value and compounder names, huge institutional buying, but Abel at Berkshire is a cuck, so this dumped 30 bucks? Ok,” one trader said. Another trader dismissed the selloff entirely and predicted further upside. “Buffets new intern guy decided to dump that doesn't mean it has to go down,” the user said. “It will be close $400 plus by end of week.” Some traders also compared the move to Berkshire’s earlier reduction in Apple shares before Apple’s subsequent rally. “UNH has a chance to run to $600 now since they sold all,” one user said. Others viewed the pullback as a buying opportunity rather than a warning sign. “This is creating a nice opportunity,” another trader said. “I’ll buy this sell off tomorrow.” UnitedHealth’s recovery has also increasingly centered around AI. The company is reportedly tracking how frequently some employees use AI tools such as ChatGPT and Microsoft Copilot as part of a broader push to integrate AI across its operations, Bloomberg reported. UnitedHealth said it has already deployed more than 1,000 AI use cases internally, with company documents reportedly showing the technology has helped avoid more than 15 million calls and process hundreds of millions of claims. CFO Wayne DeVeydt recently said AI is advancing “faster than people can appreciate or understand,” while emphasizing that the company sees a major opportunity to lead the healthcare industry through faster automation and operational efficiency. UnitedHealth plans to invest $1.5 billion into AI this year and previously said it is already generating at least a two-to-one return on those investments. Shares of critical mineral companies, including MP Materials (MP), USA Rare Earth (USAR), Energy Fuels (UUUU), and United States Antimony (UAMY), moved into focus after a new White House fact sheet signaled progress in easing U.S.-China tensions surrounding critical mineral supply chains. The White House said on Sunday that China has agreed to act on U.S. concerns about shortages in critical mineral supply chains, marking progress in ongoing trade talks between the two countries. The commitment focuses on materials essential for advanced manufacturing, defense systems, and clean energy technologies. While MP Materials, USA Rare Earth, and United States Antimony stocks were down overnight, Energy Fuels edged 0.9% higher, ahead of Monday. Beijing plans to address American concerns about the limited availability of key rare-earth elements, including yttrium, scandium, neodymium, and indium. The agreement also covers restrictions on the export and sale of equipment and technologies used in the extraction and processing of rare earths. The agreement is viewed as part of a wider push to reduce dependency on concentrated supply chains dominated by a single geography. By addressing both raw material exports and production technology controls, the deal could ease long-standing bottlenecks in industries reliant on rare earth inputs. The update follows a high-level summit in Beijing last week between U.S. President Donald Trump and his Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping. The U.S. is trying to reduce its reliance on China, which controls about 90% of the world’s processed rare earth minerals and magnets. The Trump administration is also increasing efforts to strengthen domestic supply chains for these important materials. This strong market position leaves the U.S. and its allies exposed to supply disruptions that could hurt important manufacturing industries. The U.S. government has invested in several critical mineral and rare-earth companies, including Lithium Americas, MP Materials, Critical Metals, and Trilogy Metals, to support domestic production. MP Materials, Energy Fuels, United States Antimony, and USA Rare Earth have emerged as key players in the push to create a domestic supply chain for materials used in defense systems, semiconductors, electric vehicles, and renewable energy technologies. MP Materials operates the Mountain Pass site in California, the only major rare-earth mining and processing facility in North America. It mainly produces neodymium and praseodymium, which are used to make powerful magnets for electric vehicles, robotics, and defense equipment. Energy Fuels has expanded beyond uranium production by using its White Mesa Mill in Utah to process heavy rare earth materials. United States Antimony focuses on refining antimony, a material used in military ammunition, optics, and flame-resistant products. (NIO) fell 4% in Hong Kong trading on Monday after Deutsche Bank warned that the strong early sales momentum for the newly launched Onvo L80 SUV may cool sharply once competition intensifies in China’s crowded EV market. Nio’s U.S.-listed shares snapped a three-week losing streak last week, finishing about 4% higher. Deutsche Bank expects the five-seat Onvo L80 sport utility vehicle to initially ramp up to monthly sales of around 10,000 units after production expansion, but forecasts deliveries could later normalize to 4,000 units a month as rival models enter the segment. The brokerage said the expected trajectory closely mirrors that of the Onvo L90, the larger three-row SUV launched last year under Nio’s mass-market sub-brand, CnEVPost reported. “We observed a similar volume trajectory for the ONVO L90,” Deutsche Bank said, noting that the model delivered more than 10,000 units per month during its first three months before slowing to 4,000 monthly deliveries in the following quarter. The cautionary note comes just days after Onvo officially launched the L80 in China with a starting price of 242,800 yuan ($35,750), slightly below its pre-sale pricing. Under Nio’s battery subscription program, buyers can lower the entry price to 156,800 yuan through its battery-as-a-service offering. Initial deliveries of the SUV began across 15 Chinese cities over the weekend as Nio accelerated efforts to expand its presence in the family-focused EV segment. Deutsche Bank said that the L80 enters one of the most competitive areas of China’s EV market, where it will compete directly against Li Auto’s Li i6, BYD’s Tang L EV and Xpeng’s G9. The brokerage expects fresh rival launches over the coming quarters to pressure Onvo’s delivery momentum after the initial wave of demand fades. Nio has increasingly relied on aggressive product launches to support volume growth as competition intensifies across China’s EV sector. The company is also preparing to begin pre-sales for the refreshed Onvo L60 SUV later this month, while its flagship ES9 SUV is expected to launch on May 27. The L80 shares its platform and dimensions with the larger Onvo L90, measuring more than five meters in length with a 3,110-mm wheelbase. Higher-end trims include LiDAR and Nio’s in-house Shenji autonomous driving chip, while entry-level variants use Nvidia’s Orin X processor. Despite concerns around the sustainability of the L80 launch cycle, Deutsche Bank said that Nio’s broader order trends in May have remained stable. The brokerage, citing Thinkercar data, said the company secured around 10,000 new vehicle orders in both the first and second weeks of May and expects total monthly order flow to remain flat month-over-month at 42,000 units. The company heads into earnings with improving delivery momentum across its premium lineup. Nio recently said its third-generation ES8 SUV will surpass 110,000 cumulative deliveries this week after reaching the 100,000-unit milestone less than a month ago. The company will report first-quarter earnings on May 21. The ES8 has become a major contributor to Nio’s recovery, accounting for more than half of the company’s first-quarter deliveries. Strong demand for the model helped Nio post its first-ever quarterly profit in the fourth quarter of 2025. Nio founder William Li previously said deliveries are expected to rebound steadily through May and June, driven by launches including the ES9 and the Onvo L80. (TSLA) slipped more than 1% in overnight trading heading into Monday as fresh SpaceX IPO developments reignited investor speculation around a potential Tesla-SpaceX merger after veteran tech investor Gene Munster said that the odds of a deal were greater than 50%. TSLA stock snapped a two-week winning streak last week, ending the week down more than 1%. Speculation around SpaceX’s long-awaited market debut accelerated after fresh reports emerged that the company could begin its public listing process within days, potentially setting up a June Nasdaq debut under the ticker “SPCX.” The offering is expected to target a valuation above $2 trillion and could raise as much as $75 billion, putting it on track to become the largest IPO ever. Investor excitement increased further after SpaceX reportedly completed a 5-for-1 stock split ahead of the listing, lowering the implied share price to $105 from over $500. Musk also added to the momentum over the weekend after publicly saying he has no plans to sell any SpaceX shares after the IPO. Wall Street interest around the deal has continued to build as large institutions position for the offering. BlackRock has reportedly explored investing between $5 billion and $10 billion into the IPO, while major investors including Fidelity, T. Rowe Price and Capital Group recently visited SpaceX’s Starbase and xAI facilities. Munster said in an interview with Tesla influencer Dillon Loomis on Sunday that he believes there is a “greater than 50%” chance that some form of Tesla-SpaceX merger happens within the next five years. “My sense is that the investment thesis around SpaceX is going to become a sovereign AI company,” Munster said. He called sovereign AI as controlling the full stack from energy to chip design, chip manufacturing, distribution through Starlink and the underlying models with Grok. Munster said that such a platform still lacks one critical element: physical AI. “I believe AI is at the highest, his highest level of importance,” Munster said. “I think that he does see this as an existential risk to humanity and also sees the opportunity around AI as being bigger than kind of all these sum of the parts.” While discussing the scale of a potential Tesla-SpaceX platform, Munster noted that Tesla currently carries a market value of $1.5 trillion, while SpaceX is rumored to be worth $1.7 trillion ahead of its expected IPO. “If you truly build that, my sense is it would be probably the most valuable company in the world,” Munster said. He also backed the merger idea. “I’m definitely rooting for it because I think what they’re trying to accomplish would be accelerated if they all come together,” he said. Shares of EchoStar Corporation (SATS) rallied 5% overnight heading into Monday as investors rushed into stocks with SpaceX exposure after fresh reports emerged around the space firm’s expected IPO timeline and valuation. SATS stock has now gained for three straight weeks, with last week marking its strongest performance in more than a month. Speculation around SpaceX’s long-awaited market debut increased over the weekend as investors focused on signs that the company could soon begin its public listing process as soon as this week. The Elon Musk-led space firm is expected to target a June Nasdaq listing that could value the company at over $2 trillion, potentially setting up the largest IPO ever seen on Wall Street. The IPO buzz intensified after shareholders were reportedly notified about a 5-for-1 stock split that lowered the implied per-share value ahead of the offering, which would also improve accessibility for retail investors. Musk also fueled optimism after publicly stating that he does not intend to sell any SpaceX shares. Institutional interest around the deal has also drawn attention. BlackRock has reportedly explored committing between $5 billion and $10 billion into the offering. Last year, EchoStar and SpaceX announced a $17 billion agreement for SpaceX to acquire EchoStar’s AWS-4 and H-block spectrum licenses to support Starlink’s direct-to-cell network. The original deal included up to $8.5 billion in cash and up to $8.5 billion in SpaceX stock, alongside a long-term deal to bring Starlink-powered satellite phone connectivity to EchoStar’s wireless customers. The deal later expanded after EchoStar and SpaceX amended the agreement to include additional AWS-3 spectrum licenses, lifting the total deal value to $20 billion. SEC filings also revealed that EchoStar could receive up to $11 billion in SpaceX Class A shares valued at $212 per share. During EchoStar’s March earnings call, the company openly acknowledged investor focus on SpaceX’s IPO. EchoStar Capital CEO Hamid Akhavan said that the company was considering “the possibility and the timing of a potential SpaceX IPO” while evaluating future capital-allocation decisions. Akhavan also clarified that EchoStar does not yet hold the SpaceX shares from the transaction. “We have a right to it, but we don’t have that equity yet,” he said. EchoStar Chairman Charlie Ergen struck a bullish tone on SpaceX, calling it “a one-of-a-kind company” and “the best company I’ve ever worked with in 45 years.” Ergen also said that investors may still be underestimating SpaceX’s valuation potential. “I don’t think any amount of valuation is probably crazy there,” he said. Most recently, the FCC approved EchoStar’s spectrum sale to SpaceX earlier this month, clearing a major regulatory hurdle for the deal and further fueling investor excitement around EchoStar’s growing SpaceX exposure. The SpaceX narrative around EchoStar has also fueled the view that SATS is becoming a retail proxy trade for the private aerospace company ahead of its public debut. Last week, New Street Research launched coverage on several space-economy companies and rated EchoStar a ‘Buy,’ specifically calling the company a “proxy play” on SpaceX due to its equity exposure. The developments come even as EchoStar’s core businesses remain under pressure. MoffettNathanson analysts said that the company was trading more like a “space-themed hedge fund” based on investor perceptions around SpaceX and future investment returns than its traditional satellite-TV and wireless operations. EchoStar itself also acknowledged the influence of the SpaceX deal in its SEC filing: “Investor expectations regarding our potential investment in SpaceX may be currently influencing our stock price, and, if so, any adverse developments relating to SpaceX, changes in market perception of SpaceX or failure to complete the SpaceX Transaction could materially and negatively impact the market price of our Class A common stock.” On Stocktwits, retail sentiment for SATS was ‘extremely bullish’ amid ‘high’ message volume. title: Coming Up Dry - unh.edu
content: At the end of a dry summer, John Moulton ’74, of Moulton Farm in Meredith, looks at his irrigation pond. Though it’s down from the high-water mark, there’s still plenty of water for him to draw. He says that’s due to changes in irrigation and planting strategies promoted by UNH Extension, including the use of drip irrigation placed under a biodegradable mulch. If he were still relying on overhead watering, as he did when he first started, his pond would be dry by now. “We’ve been irrigating many of our crops, and right now we’re still looking at 8 or 900,000 gallons of water out of a total capacity of 1.2 million,” Moulton says. “Years ago, we would have drained that pond by this time.” Moulton’s need for a new approach to irrigation, shared by farmers and gardeners across the state, is a result of a dry 2026. It can no longer be called abnormally dry, though, because weather data show dry summers are becoming more common in New England. Though not traditionally thought of as a dry climate, recent experience has shown that drought is no longer a rare event in New Hampshire. The state’s Department of Environmental Services reports that drought occurred 11 times between 2000 and 2020, and that as of August of 2026, parts of Rockingham and Strafford counties have been experiencing moderate drought for 12 months and counting. It is time for New Englanders to bone up on gardening in drought conditions. The irrigation pond at Moulton Farm in Meredith holds about 1.2 million gallons of water. While the effects of dry conditions are most apparent above ground, as leaves wilt and stems droop, some of the more concerning things are happening at the plant’s roots. “There are several layers of how drought impacts soil and plant health,” says Renuka Mathur, UNH Extension’s soil health state specialist. To explain drought’s effects on soil, Mathur starts by noting specific elements of soil, including organic matter, as well as the mycorrhizal fungus and microbes that decompose the organic residue and make nutrients available to nearby roots. Dry conditions can reduce the activity of fungus and microbes, making for less nutrient availability to plants. Prolonged drought can kill off the fungus and microbes, meaning that soil will be less active when moisture returns. “If fungus and microbes die, they don’t bounce back immediately,” Mathur says. It can take several seasons, she adds, and the mix of microbes might be different when they do return. “Sometimes the damage of the drought can be permanent.” If the microbes and fungi aren’t delivering nutrition, it might be tempting to use fertilizers, Mathur says, but doing so in drought conditions comes with hazards. Without rainfall and accompanied by high temperatures, the fertilizer, typically applied as a salt compound, can concentrate on leaves or the soil surface, leading to burn injuries for the plant. “If you want to fertilize, do so in the evening or early morning so the salt injury risk is reduced,” Mathur says. She also warns against excessive tilling, because it exposes more moisture to evaporation, and has other negative effects. “When you till dry soil, it breaks the structure of the soil and causes rapid decomposition of organic residue in the soil,” Mathur says. “Add a little bit of rain or wind, and it causes fine disrupted soil to re-settle, creating a cementing effect. It does so in a dense layer that prevents water absorption and encourages water and nutrient runoff.” Instead of tilling, Mathur suggests mulching — placing a layer of some material on top of the soil, often done as a weed control measure. Mulch also has the benefit of keeping moisture levels higher in the soil. If there were a mulch fan club, Sean O’Brien, home horticulture program manager for Extension, could campaign to be its president. “I advocate for mulch all the time, for lots of reasons but certainly moisture loss is a big one,” O’Brien says. He suggests using “whatever you have abundantly” to mulch, whether it’s fallen leaves, straw, pine needles, or even cardboard. Many commercial growers will use plastic, but home growers might prefer a material that will break down in the soil at the end of the growing season and become next year’s organic matter. The presence of organic matter in soil will help it to retain moisture. O’Brien says they recommend organic matter content of 4 to 10%, and Extension offers soil testing for those who want to know precisely. While you’re mulching, it might be a good time to think about your irrigation strategy. Watering with a sprinkler or by hand is the easiest to set up, but “overhead watering,” as O’Brien terms it, is problematic. Some of the water evaporates before it’s absorbed by the soil, it can encourage disease spread through splashing, and is often associated with under-watering. Drip irrigation or soaker hoses, ideally placed underneath the mulch layer, ensure that the water goes where the roots can reach it — while minimizing water use. To that point, O’Brien says that irrigation frequency and volume are important considerations. Water less often, but soak the soil when you do, he says, which will train your plants to grow long roots. “You want to make sure you’re watering deeply and less frequently, that will help your plants to weather those drier conditions.” When planning your garden, select plant varieties that are drought resistant, says. O’Brien, who notes that there are varieties of just about every plant that can handle a dry spell. “Drought is something that we’re going to have to deal with for the foreseeable future,” O’Brien says.“For gardeners, it’s the new frontier.” Regular and extended drought might be a new problem for New Hampshire gardeners. Thankfully, local gardeners have adaptability — as well as expertise from UNH Extension — to keep their gardens green. Copyright © 2026 , University of New Hampshire. All rights reserved.

title: Unlocking the Outdoors - unh.edu
content: Everyone should be able to take a stroll — or a roll — through the woods in New Hampshire, believe the folks behind the website Trail Finder. For those who have ability limitations, though, starting down a trail can be a gamble, as it’s hard to know exactly what kind of terrain is around the next bend. The odds are turning in their favor, thanks to a partnership between UNH Extension and Trail Finder. As a result of that partnership, Brendan Thornton ’27 spent his summer surveying and documenting the accessibility of trails throughout the state. Thornton gathered data on 29 trails this year, bringing the total number of surveyed trails to 56 so far. Trail Finder’s effort to make trails more welcoming to more people began several years ago, when they added the ability for trails to be marked as “accessible.” That was a solution that invited more questions than it answered, they found. The problem with the initial strategy used by Trail Finder’s designers, said Stephen Engle, executive director of Community Geographics, a digital mapping technology company that joined with Extension and the Upper Valley Trails Alliance to create the platform in 2010, was that it used a simplistic approach to accessibility. In that first attempt, a trail network was considered either accessible or not, and it was left up to the trail owner or manager to make the call. Results were uneven at best, Engle says. A trail might be listed as accessible even though there was a curb between the parking lot and trail head. Or, in other cases, a largely accessible network was not marked as such because the trail manager felt uncertain. “On the whole, we felt that Trail Finder wasn’t doing the best job in helping users find trails to meet their ability,” says Engle. They needed a new approach, one that leans into the quirks and features of each individual trail. Each trail has its own aspects of accessibility, such as incline, trail surface, and restroom facilities. Each hiker has their unique physical limitations, and a trail that’s accessible to one person might be hazardous for someone else. “Everybody has their own perception. There are differing interpretations of what accessible means.” When talking about barriers to trail access, says UNH Extension Specialist Emma Tutein, a lack of information might be the first hurdle. “Where is the trail, what is it like, how do we even get to it?” Tutein says. “For a lot of people, they want to know. And that becomes more important if you have a disability.” The problem is, gathering all that data takes time and expertise. A solution was found in 2025 when a UNH student, interning with Extension, spent his summer examining trails for their surface material, width, degree of incline, cross-slope, and amenities such as benches and accessible restrooms. The NH Charitable Foundation provides funding for the project. This summer, that cache of information doubled in size, thanks to the efforts of Brendan Thornton ’27, an environmental conservation and sustainability major who has been exploring New Hampshire woods since he was a toddler. “This job is cool because I get to use my love for nature and the outdoors ,” Thornton says, “and apply my skills to helping people who might not have the same opportunities as me.” One of Thornton’s relatives has Down syndrome, so he already understood the importance of inclusion. Working on the trail project gave him new insight, however. He was studying a trail in North Conway when a man stopped and told him about his wife, who has trouble navigating certain trails due to nerve damage, although her disability is invisible to most. “Knowing that I’m helping people like that is pretty cool,” Thornton says. “It’s definitely something I think about when I’m out there.” Engle says that people with disabilities are used to encountering physical barriers, but sometimes informational barriers are the hardest to overcome. No one wants to make it halfway down a trail only to find an unexpected stream crossing, gate or boulder blocking their progress. “One of the most important things for us to understand is that having detailed information about trails benefits everyone. But we haven’t taken the time to curate our trails to the levels that people really needed,” Engle says. That’s now changing, he adds, with the growing list of trail networks that are built, or re-built, to be accessible to all users. And it’s also changing through the work of people like Thornton, who says he wants everyone to be able to access the benefits of trail walking. “It slows me down and it makes me appreciate what’s going on around me,” Thornton says. “It’s a place where there’s no noise, your head’s clear, and you don’t have anything going on except looking around to see nature’s beauty. That experience should be accessible to everyone.” Copyright © 2026 , University of New Hampshire. All rights reserved.

title: Why Is UNH Stock Trading At A Premium With The Slowest Growth? - Trefis
content: UnitedHealth (UNH) runs the best operating margin of the three managed care companies in its peer group, and the slowest revenue growth of the three. It also carries a significant valuation premium over its peer, Cigna, trading at more than double its earnings multiple. The headline margin spread reflects UnitedHealth’s higher-margin Optum services mix as much as underwriting efficiency. What the current valuation assumes is that this consolidated edge holds. The size of the premium is clearest against Cigna. UnitedHealth trades at 25.6 times trailing net earnings on a 4.8% operating margin—though its raised 2026 guidance brings that multiple closer to 21 times forward earnings. Cigna trades at 11.3 times trailing net earnings on 3.2%. CVS trades at 25.1 times, but on trailing earnings that include at least one loss quarter, so it does not compare with a clean year. The premium is not buying revenue growth. UnitedHealth’s revenue grew 6.5% over the last twelve months, the slowest in the group, against Cigna’s 7.7%. Nor is the premium buying the group’s highest trailing return—CVS delivered 34.3% against UnitedHealth’s 30.5%—even as both soundly beat the S&P 500’s managed care index over the same stretch. The stock also sits about 33% below its two-year high. Not only in the health plan. UnitedHealthcare is guided to at least $12 billion of operating earnings for 2026, against about $25.45 billion guided for the whole company. Revenue over the trailing twelve months was $450.13 billion, the base the 4.8% trailing margin is measured against, and the 2026 guidance is what shows where those earnings come from. The lead is earned beside the insurance book as well as inside it. The rest sits in Optum. Optum Rx, the pharmacy benefit business, is guided to $6.25 billion of operating earnings for 2026 on its own, and management has been rebuilding it around monthly per-member fees. Management expects to end 2026 with more than 95% of clients on full pass-through of manufacturer rebates. Optum Health, the care delivery arm, cares for 20 million people through primary and specialist care, ambulatory surgery and home health. Management raised its 2026 adjusted earnings per share guidance to a range of $19.50 to $20.00, up from greater than $18.25. The test is the second half of 2026, now underway, when earnings tilt heavily toward Optum Rx and Optum Insight to make up for UnitedHealthcare’s front-loaded year. The pressure sits in the commercial book. Management says medical cost trends there are running modestly above 11%, higher than planned, and full commercial margin recovery to its target 7%-plus range remains pushed past 2027, as management previously indicated. One driver is the arbitration process under the No Surprises Act, which management says is adding about 50 basis points of incremental cost trend in 2026, with management noting that roughly 60% of cases are driven by just five entities. UnitedHealthcare is opening its front door wider at the same time. From October 1 a broad range of conditions no longer needs prior approval, part of a plan to eliminate 30% of its prior authorization volume by the end of 2026. At 25.6 times earnings, the stock’s valuation prices in a margin lead that the commercial book is still working to recover, paired with the group’s slowest top-line growth. BREAKING: Stocks Fall For Week On $100 Oil, Surging Yields Despite Friday Bounce CVS Health (CVS) noted a continuation of "high-trend" medical cost growth at a Wells Fargo investor conference on Wednesday, helping to put a spring in the step of hospital stocks including HCA Healthcare (HCA), while souring the mood of managed care investors. Shares of CVS stock came away relatively unscathed, while UnitedHealth (UNH) slipped and Oscar Health (OSCR) stumbled. CVS management's comments about medical cost trends were brief and vague, while Wells Fargo conference presentations by HCA and Universal Health Services (UHS) didn't appear to provide updates to Q3 trends since Q2 earnings calls. However, CVS did highlight "pockets of favorability, particularly in Medicare," according to a preliminary transcript from FactSet that didn't clearly identify the speakers. Here's the full CVS quote, apparently from Aetna President Steve Nelson: "We don't see them (the trends) necessarily going down. We see some pockets of favorability, particularly in Medicare. But it's a high-trend environment. So, we remain cautious, prudent in kind of how we're thinking about things because we need to finish the job of getting our business back to target margin." Meanwhile, both UHS and HCA executives hit on a similar theme that didn't appear to diverge from their Q2 updates. Both said that a key dynamic has been the drop in ACA Marketplace coverage after the expiration of enhanced premium subsidies at the end of 2025. Both hospital groups indicated that many of those who lost coverage joined the ranks of the uninsured rather than transitioning to Medicaid or employer coverage, resulting in more unpaid bills. Based on the CVS comments, it's not surprising that Medicare-focused Humana (HUM) has outperformed the medical managed care group, edging down 0.45% in afternoon trade. Although UnitedHealth Group is the largest Medicare Advantage provider, shares fell 2%, likely reflecting its broad membership in Medicaid and commercial coverage. CVS stock dipped 0.7%. Centene (CNC), the biggest ACA insurer by members as well as a big Medicaid provider and growing player in Medicare, dipped 0.2%. Oscar was the big loser, falling 4.7%, though it found support at its 50-day line. Oscar's greater volatility may be partially a reflection of its relatively strong stock performance this year. Further, the CVS comments highlight the same uncertainty that contributed to selling pressure in July and August. Oscar's ACA enrollment soared this year, even as overall enrollment tumbled. Further, Oscar's membership appears to be on the younger, healthier side, with members who gravitated to lower-cost bronze plans. Based on its relatively healthy risk pool, Oscar expects about 20% of its premiums will be paid out via risk adjustment to other carriers under ACA rules. However, if ACA benefit costs run high, risk-adjustment payments could take a bigger bite of its profits. Stocks Fall On Oil, Yields, But Meta Jumps. Inflation Data Due. title: Are There Links Between Dairy Consumption and Depression? - unh.edu
content: Depression is a complex disease that can be difficult to identify, but nearly one in five Americans has received a diagnosis for depression and one in 20 are affected by depression symptoms on a daily basis. A wide variety of factors can underlie depression and depressive symptoms, but new research at UNH indicates that dairy products do not contribute to worse depressive symptoms in a group of people previously documented to be at a particularly high risk for depression. It further suggests that yogurt and butter in particular may be beneficial. Consumption of dairy products with higher fat content, including yogurt and butter, was associated with fewer depressive symptoms. Dairy consumption is recommended as part of a healthy diet by the U.S. Dietary Guidelines for Americans. Dairy includes a unique profile of fatty acids, along with other nutrients, that may benefit inflammation. There is concern over the recommendation of consuming full-fat dairy products, however, due to saturated fat content. Yet the potential impacts of dairy, including those with fat, on depression, a leading cause of poor quality of life, is limited. A study published in Nutrients and led by Sherman Bigornia, associate professor in the Department of Agriculture, Nutrition, and Food Systems in the College of Life Sciences and Agriculture (COLSA), looked at the association of total dairy consumption as well as individual dairy products — milk, cheese, yogurt, cream, and butter — with depressive symptoms in Hispanic/Latino adults over a six-year period. The team, which included researchers from nine institutions, used data from the Hispanic Community Health Study/Study of Latinos (HCHS/SOL), an ongoing longitudinal study of 16,415 Hispanic/Latino adults living in the U.S. Evidence suggests Hispanic/Latino adults experience high rates of depression, and they also have a disproportionate burden of obesity and metabolic syndrome, both characterized by chronic inflammation. Chronic inflammation, cardiovascular dysfunction, and metabolic syndrome have all been implicated in depression. Researchers from HCHS/SOL collected participants’ baseline dietary information and also assessed depressive symptoms using a validated survey scale at the initial visit and again during a follow-up clinical exam six years later. A total of 10,618 participants provided complete data for analysis. The Bigornia team, including first author Anne Bodenrader ’26G, used the data to identify and estimate daily dairy product consumption and analyzed associations with depressive symptoms. The team found that total dairy consumption was not significantly associated with depressive symptoms over the six-year period. Individual dairy products showed some potentially important differences, however. While milk, cheese, and cream consumption were not significantly associated with the score, yogurt and butter consumption were both significantly associated with fewer depressive symptoms. The effect sizes were very small, underscoring the need for cautious interpretation and further study, but both yogurt and butter have biological properties that make beneficial effects plausible. title: UNH Stock Drops 3.2%—Is the 36% Six-Month Rebound Overpriced? - TechStock²
content: UnitedHealth Group shares were down 3.2% at $387.97 at 10:33 a.m. Eastern time Wednesday, but the stock is hardly back in bargain territory. It remains 36.1% above its March 9 close and now trades at about 19.6 times the midpoint of management’s 2026 adjusted-earnings guidance. The answer for investors is conditional: UNH can justify that multiple if its medical-cost recovery is durable and the July guidance increase holds. It looks expensive if membership contraction and favorable reserve development are doing more of the work than recurring operating improvement. Delayed NYSE data put UnitedHealth at $387.97, down from Tuesday’s $400.84 close. The company had not issued a new earnings release or filed a market-moving disclosure Wednesday morning. The move came during a broad selloff as Brent crude pushed above $100 and the Dow fell roughly 0.8% shortly after the open, according to Associated Press market coverage. That makes the decline a poor standalone verdict on UnitedHealth’s business. The more useful comparison is the six-month rerating. From $285.17 on March 9 to Wednesday’s intraday price, UNH has gained 36.1%. It has recovered much of the discount created by medical-cost pressure, Medicare Advantage funding concerns and the reset in earnings expectations. UnitedHealth’s July outlook calls for adjusted earnings of $19.50 to $20.00 per share in 2026. Dividing Wednesday’s $387.97 price by the $19.75 midpoint produces a forward multiple of 19.6. The midpoint is 20.8% above the $16.35 adjusted EPS reported for 2025. That is not an extreme valuation for a dominant health insurer and services company, but it is no longer a distressed multiple. Buyers are paying for a large portion of the earnings repair before the full-year result is delivered. The second quarter supplied evidence for the rebound. Revenue was $112.0 billion, operating earnings reached $8.0 billion and adjusted EPS was $6.38. Operating earnings rose from $5.2 billion a year earlier, while the medical care ratio improved to 86.7% from 89.4%. Full-year adjusted-EPS guidance moved to $19.50–$20.00 from the “greater than $17.75” floor issued in January. Cash generation gives the recovery substance. UnitedHealth produced $11.1 billion of operating cash flow in the second quarter and guided to about $24 billion for 2026. It had repurchased $4.0 billion of stock through mid-July and expects at least $5.0 billion for the year, according to the earnings materials filed with the SEC. The board also declared a $2.32 quarterly dividend payable September 22 to holders of record on September 14. At Wednesday’s intraday price, four quarterly payments at that rate imply a 2.4% annualized yield. The combination of buybacks, dividends and debt reduction can support per-share value even while consolidated revenue grows slowly. Second-quarter revenue was only 0.4% above the prior-year period. UnitedHealthcare served 48.5 million medical members, 1.6 million fewer than a year earlier. Medicare Advantage membership fell 9% to 7.565 million, and management said seniors served through Medicare Advantage had contracted by 965,000 since year-end. Optum Health had a similar trade-off. Revenue fell 5% as the business served roughly 700,000 fewer value-based-care patients, although operating earnings improved to $1.2 billion and its margin reached 5.1%. Pricing, benefit redesign and market exits are restoring profitability, but they are also reducing the customer base available for future growth. Earnings quality deserves attention too. UnitedHealth disclosed $860 million of favorable prior-period medical reserve development in the quarter. That does not invalidate the margin improvement, but reserve releases are not a growth engine investors can simply repeat each quarter. At nearly 20 times guided adjusted earnings, the market needs cost control to remain effective after that support fades. The first test is the medical care ratio. Management’s full-year target is 88.1%, plus or minus 25 basis points. A result above that range would suggest care utilization or provider pricing is outrunning premiums. The second is enrollment: further Medicare Advantage and value-based-care contraction could leave UnitedHealth relying on margin expansion rather than balanced growth. Regulation remains a valuation discount, not a footnote. In its second-quarter 10-Q, UnitedHealth said it was responding to government subpoenas, information requests and investigations, including reviews involving Medicare risk-adjustment coding. It said the scope and outcome could not be assured. Medicare Advantage rates also remain below the company’s estimate of forward medical-cost trends. After Wednesday’s drop, UNH is less expensive than it was Tuesday, but the stock is not priced for another operational stumble. A sustainable medical-cost ratio, stable membership and clean cash conversion would make 19.6 times guidance defensible. If the next results show renewed cost pressure or deeper enrollment losses, the six-month rally leaves considerably more downside than it did in March. Choose company and market-topic hubs. For years, the race to build better artificial intelligence centered on making models bigger, feeding them more data, and expanding the amount of information they could process at once. Now, a fresh frontier is emerging as researchers increasingly explore smarter memory management as another way to build more capable AI systems. Two academic papers published this month, AutoMem and SelfMem, argue that memory shouldn't be a rigid feature engineered by developers using static rules. Instead, they propose that AI systems can learn to manage their own memories. They take different approaches: AutoMem trains AI to manage an external memory system, while SelfMem lets agents refine their own memory strategies through feedback, and both report substantial gains on long-horizon benchmarks. Imagine working with an AI coding assistant on a project for months. Instead of repeatedly reminding it about your project's architecture and coding style, a smarter memory system could retain the decisions that matter while discarding obsolete information. Researchers believe that this kind of selective memory will become increasingly important as AI agents take on longer-running tasks. One way developers have tried to build more capable chatbots is by expanding their context windows, which are the immediate digital scratchpad an AI considers during a conversation. While larger context windows let models process more information, they also increase computational costs and don't necessarily help AI distinguish useful information from irrelevant details. The papers instead explore an alternative approach based on active memory curation. In AutoMem, Stanford University researchers introduced a memory manager that decides when to create, update, search, and delete records, allowing the AI to maintain a compact memory instead of continuously accumulating information. Tested on grueling, complex video games like NetHack and Crafter, this memory-management approach slashed the agent's memory growth rate by 95% and doubled its task performance, allowing a 32-billion-parameter open-weight model to perform competitively with frontier models including Claude Opus 4.5 and Gemini 3.1 Pro Thinking on the evaluated long-horizon benchmarks. SelfMem takes a completely parameter-free approach. Instead of editing model weights, it gives the AI a dedicated workspace and tools to inspect an unchangeable transcript store. It allows the agent to inspect, write, review, and revise its own memory, outperforming traditional retrieval pipelines by more than 40% on the BEAM benchmark while using only a fraction of the computational cost. The push for smarter memory comes as AI companies shift from one-off chatbots to autonomous agents designed to work over days or weeks. Whether writing software, tracking supply chains, or managing research projects, these systems must retain relevant information while discarding details that no longer matter. That is where autonomous memory management changes the equation. Instead of forcing a user to repeatedly copy-paste instructions, an agent equipped with an optimized memory workflow seamlessly recalls structural boundaries, tracks cumulative progress, and discards transient data that is no longer relevant. Better memory could also reduce the computational cost of repeatedly processing the same information, a potential advantage as AI companies look to deploy agents more efficiently at scale. Over the past year, leading AI companies like OpenAI, Google, and Anthropic have introduced basic memory features, allowing consumer chatbots to retain user preferences and custom instructions across distinct chat sessions. Today's commercial memory features generally rely on predefined mechanisms for deciding what information is retained. AutoMem and SelfMem instead point toward AI systems capable of independently evaluating and regulating their own memories. As tech companies race to build AI systems capable of executing truly long-horizon work, the findings suggest memory management may become an increasingly important complement to larger models. Future AI systems may be judged not only by how much they know, but also by how effectively they decide what information is worth keeping. Lucid Motors (LCID) shares rose for a second straight day on Thursday after the electric vehicle maker forcefully rejected reports that it was considering bankruptcy or a take-private transaction, rebounding from a brutal selloff earlier in the week. The stock traded 12% higher at the time of writing and is on track to clock its best week since July 2025, thanks to a 29% jump on Wednesday, if gains hold. The stock’s dramatic rise and fall started after an Electric-Vehicles.com report on Tuesday said that restructuring adviser AlixPartners has outlined scenarios to the company’s board, including taking the company private or seeking Chapter 11 protection. The stock fell as much as 50% on the news, but pared gains after the company refuted the report as “completely false.” “The company has sufficient liquidity to carry its operations well into next year, as recently published in its last quarterly filings, and it has not formed any special Board committee to explore the scenarios reported today,” Lucid said in a statement to Stocktwits. It also added that AlixPartners is only assisting the company to improve operational performance and did not advise Lucid on a take-private transaction or bankruptcy. They further didn't suggest either option to the company management or board, it added. The company also delivered a cease and desist letter to the publication stating that the company “unequivocally denies the central factual assertions” in the article. Lucid’s new CEO, Silvio Napoli, also said in a post on LinkedIn that the claims circulated were “far from the facts” and that he looks forward to providing a full update on its quarterly earnings call on August 4. Lucid, majority-owned by Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund (PIF), has faced significant headwinds as an electric vehicle maker. Earlier this month, the company reported second-quarter production of 4,774 vehicles and deliveries of 3,953 units— marking a modest year-over-year increase but short of analyst expectations amid slower-than-hoped demand for the new Gravity SUV. The results coincided with a sweeping leadership overhaul under CEO Silvio Napoli, who assumed the role in June. Napoli replaced CFO Taoufiq Boussaid with automotive finance veteran Alexander De Bock, appointed new executives for technology, customer, digital, and transformation roles, flattened the reporting structure by halving direct reports to the CEO, and eliminated the COO position. These moves followed June layoffs of roughly 1,500 employees, about 18% of the workforce, and the removal of a second production shift at the Arizona plant, aimed at delivering roughly $158 million in annual savings. Financially, Lucid continues to face steep losses and negative gross margins despite revenue growth. In the first quarter, it posted revenue of $282.5 million, up 20% year-over-year, but recorded a net loss of approximately $1.03 billion. The company has relied heavily on its majority shareholder, Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund, for support. It raised about $1.05 billion in April, including $550 million in preferred stock from PIF, $200 million from Uber, and a public offering, and drew an additional $800 million from an existing delayed-draw term loan facility in early July. (Bloomberg) -- UnitedHealth Group Inc. has sold an interest in some of its Optum Health operations in Florida to private equity company TPG Inc. as the health conglomerate is working to recover from a collapse in profits last year. Apple's $2,000-Plus Foldable iPhone Was a Decade in the Making EU and Canada Plan Far-Reaching Alliance to Strengthen Partnership Indonesia's Richest Family Moves More Than $1 Billion Offshore Sapporo Beer Moving Production to US From Canada on Tariffs Canada Hits US Imports With Tariffs, Intensifying Trade War "We didn't need the dollars, we have the dollars to invest, but we needed the focus and somebody that could actually work with us locally," UnitedHealth Chief Financial Officer Wayne DeVeydt said in an interview with Bloomberg News. Working with TPG will allow the business to grow more quickly than it would be able to if UnitedHealth were running everything while also executing a broader turnaround, he said. UnitedHealth is in the midst of reorienting its business after it unexpectedly reported disappointing profit last year, driven by failures in its Optum Health division, which runs the medical clinics. Optum Health's operating margins were negative that year as healthcare costs rose and federal policies restricted payments. The company replaced its chief executive officer and other leaders in the wake of the weak results. Optum Health margins will be around 2% this year, higher than previously expected, because the company is rolling out programs more quickly, DeVeydt said. Margins should increase to around 4% in 2027 and 6% the following year, he said. The Florida clinics are part of Optum's WellMed business, which focuses on healthcare for older people. UnitedHealth is opening about 15 clinics a year in Florida, DeVeydt said. The Optum WellMed TPG partnership started within the last year. "We actually brought in a partner so we could make some more investment in the market and be positioned for strategic growth," Optum Health CEO Krista Nelson said. TPG also bought Optum UK, a different UnitedHealth subsidiary, earlier this year, according to media reports. UnitedHealth said the sale of Optum UK generated $400 million for the United Health Foundation. UnitedHealth also expects to reaffirm its financial guidance Wednesday at an investor conference hosted by Wells Fargo & Co., DeVeydt said.
